claims.text: Tourism is travel away from a person's usual home for leisure, business, sport or visiting friends and family, normally involving at least one night away. The receiving area is the place the tourist travels to, which earns income from their spending.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: World tourism grew from about 25 million international arrivals in 1950 to about 1 400 million in 2019 (rounded figures), because cheaper air travel, rising incomes, paid holidays from work and easier booking through package tours and the internet gave far more people the money, the time and the means to travel.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Attractions come from the physical landscape and the human landscape, and each draws particular visitors: a sheltered beach and a hot dry winter climate suit swimming and sunbathing, a coral reef suits diving, mountains suit hiking, waterholes full of wildlife suit game viewing, while historic buildings, museums, festivals and local crafts draw sightseers and cultural visitors.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Listing attractions without saying why they attract is a list, not an explanation: each attraction earns credit when it is described together with the visitors it draws - a coral reef attracts divers, and a hot dry winter climate attracts sun-seekers. The test: does each attraction say what the visitor does there?

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Tourism benefits a receiving area through jobs - direct jobs in hotels, restaurants and guiding, and indirect jobs in farming, crafts, building and transport that supply them - and through foreign income, because visitors' spending is money earned outside and spent inside the area, like an export; it can also bring roads, water supplies and airports that local people share.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Tourism also brings problems: much of the work is seasonal and low paid, money leaks away to foreign-owned airlines, hotel chains and tour operators, land and food prices can rise for local people in the busy season, and crowds bring congestion, litter, footpath erosion and habitat disturbance.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Impacts of tourism are sorted by who or what feels them: local people feel jobs, wages, prices, crowding and cultural change, while the environment feels erosion, litter and habitat loss. The test: people or environment? Writing about the natural environment when the question asks about local people, or the reverse, misses the question.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Sustainable tourism meets the needs of visitors, the tourist industry and local people today without reducing the ability of future visitors and residents to meet theirs, which means protecting the landscape, wildlife and culture that attract the visitors in the first place.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Management strategies keep tourism sustainable: caps on visitor numbers, entry and conservation fees that fund protection, boardwalks and marked trails that concentrate damage on a hardened line, and local ownership through community conservancies or partnerships, so a fair share of the income stays with the people who host the visitors.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Careful management is required because unmanaged tourism destroys its own attraction: eroded paths, disturbed wildlife, litter and crowding drive visitors away, so the industry declines unless the environment and the community that carry it are protected.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Etosha National Park in northern Namibia covers about 22 000 square kilometres of dry woodland and grassland around a vast salt pan, with state rest camps at Okaukuejo, Halali and Namutoni each built beside an artificial waterhole where elephants, lions, giraffes and the park's black rhinos come to drink; the park received roughly 200 000 visitors a year in the late 2010s (rounded figure).

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Tourism is important to the Etosha area because park conservation fees and rest-camp wages are a foundation of a dry region with few other employers, and because neighbouring communal conservancies - registered areas where a community holds the rights to manage and benefit from its wildlife - receive levies from joint-venture lodges, so the income reaches villages outside the gates.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Management at Etosha caps the beds in its three state rest camps rather than allowing unlimited building, charges day visitors a conservation fee, and enforces speed limits and a ban on off-road driving, so wildlife and the salt pan are protected while the visits that pay for that protection continue.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).
